title: The Metropolitan Police explores AI to grade and triage child sexual abuse imagery so that officers can find unknown victims faster
summary: The Metropolitan Police said on 13 April 2026 that it is testing unnamed companies' AI tools to grade abuse imagery and flag unknown victims; no use on live cases is reported.
account: On 12 July 2019 the Home Office announced an image categorization algorithm for the national Child Abuse Image Database. On 13 April 2026 the Metropolitan Police Service announced that it is exploring a similar use of artificial intelligence: rapid grading and triage of child sexual abuse imagery. Material possibly relating to unknown victims could then be flagged for prioritized safeguarding. The force also wants to reduce officers' manual review of distressing material. It said that it is in conversations with multiple companies. It said that it is testing how this could work. It described a separate tool that reviews 641,000 messages in 35 minutes. It also described a £10 million investment in victim interview suites. It cited more than 5,400 child sexual abuse offenses investigated in the past year and over 1,300 children safeguarded. Deputy Commissioner Matt Jukes said that speed matters for safeguarding. He said that human judgment and oversight would remain central. The OECD AI Incidents Monitor records the announcement as an “AI hazard” and notes that the use is under consideration and not implemented. As of 29 October 2026 neither the Metropolitan Police nor the OECD monitor had reported any use of the grading tools on live cases or any result.
purpose: Rapidly analyze seized imagery to grade it in categories A to C. Flag content possibly showing previously unknown victims. The aims are to prioritize safeguarding and reduce officer exposure.
